question:
Could a closed-source frontier vision-language model (GPT-5-class, Gemini 2.5/3-class, Claude-class) or a very large open-weight VLM (e.g. Qwen-VL 72B-class, InternVL 78B-class) used with prompting (zero-shot, rubric prompts, few-shot in-context exemplars) improve a no-reference image-quality defect grader beyond what fine-tuned vision encoders achieve, and if so is it better used (a) as a teacher whose labels or soft scores are distilled into small student models, or (b) as a judge / grading model that adjudicates severity or re-labels noisy training labels?

Context to hold fixed: the task is single-frame no-reference quality assessment of processed/enhanced short-video frames. Six defect types are labelled independently: blur, texture loss, over-sharpening, corruption/glitch, "over-generation" (hallucinated or painted-looking texture invented by AI restoration / super-resolution), and abrupt artificial background blur (cut-out look). Each has an ordinal severity grade (severe / medium / mild / none). Only about 3,500 human-labelled frames exist; an ensemble of fine-tuned vision encoders (RADIO, PE-Core, SigLIP2-class towers plus a fine-tuned 8B VLM) already detects the defects well (detection AUC about 0.95) but grades severity poorly (adjacent-grade AUC about 0.80; about 0.70 for over-generation), and human annotators themselves are inconsistent on adjacent grades. The metric is a macro-F1 over defect-by-severity labels plus a recall-weighted score for the severe grade. The deployed model must run on one 24 GB GPU within 15 seconds per image, so a very large or API model could realistically only be used offline (labelling, distillation, adjudication) unless evidence says it is worth the deployment cost.

Questions to answer with published evidence (2023-2026): 
1. How accurate are frontier closed-source VLMs and the largest open-weight VLMs, zero-shot or few-shot, at low-level visual perception: identifying distortion type and, separately, grading distortion severity (Q-Bench / Q-Bench+, Q-Instruct, Co-Instruct, DepictQA / DepictQA-Wild, Q-Align, DistortBench, AIGC / super-resolution artifact benchmarks, NTIRE 2024-2025 quality-assessment and AIGC-quality challenges)? How do they compare with humans and with fine-tuned specialist IQA models, especially for fine-grained severity and for AI-restoration artifacts?
2. Is there evidence that pseudo-labels, soft scores or rationales from a large VLM, distilled into a small student, improve quality-assessment or fine-grained ordinal grading when a few thousand human labels already exist? Under what conditions does VLM-teacher distillation fail (teacher weaker than the fine-tuned student, label-convention mismatch)?
3. Is there evidence for VLM-as-judge use: adjudicating between two candidate grades, pairwise comparison of two images ("which is more degraded"), re-labelling or filtering noisy ordinal labels, or few-shot in-context grading with labelled exemplars and a written rubric? Does pairwise / comparative prompting work better than absolute grading for VLMs?
4. Practical constraints: cost and latency of API VLMs at image resolutions that preserve fine texture (does down-scaling by the API destroy the evidence?), known failure modes of VLMs on low-level detail, and whether fine-tuning a large open VLM on a few thousand labels beats prompting.
Conclude with which use (none, teacher/distillation, judge/adjudicator, in-context grader) has the strongest evidence of adding accuracy in this setting, and what a cheap pilot experiment to test it would look like.
summary: Published evidence from 2023-2026 does not show that a closed-source frontier VLM, or a larger open VLM, grades defect severity better by prompting than a fine-tuned ensemble. On the one benchmark that tests joint distortion type and severity with current models (DistortBench, April 2026), the best model is a Qwen-family 27B at 61.9%, about level with individual humans, while GPT-5.4 scores 51.6%. Accuracy is lowest at the middle grades and on restoration-type artifacts, which is where this project is already weak. Wherever in-domain labels exist, fine-tuned specialists (small encoders or 7-8B VLMs) beat prompted frontier models by wide margins. Of the offline uses, the best supported is a pairwise judge that adjudicates adjacent-grade labels against anchor frames; teacher distillation has evidence only where no human labels existed, and in-context grading has no surviving evidence, so a small held-out pilot should come before any labelling or distillation spend.

findings.claim: Zero-shot, current VLMs identify distortion type and severity at roughly untrained-human level, not above it, and neither closed-source status nor parameter count predicts who does best. No published result shows a closed-source model beating a Qwen-family 27B on this skill.
findings.vote: 3-0 on merged claims 0, 2, 3 and 8; 2-1 on claim 1 (closed-source gives no advantage)
findings.evidence: DistortBench (13,500 four-choice questions, 27 synthetic distortions, 5 severity levels, 18 VLMs): the best model, Qwen3.5 27B, reaches 61.9%. Human majority vote is 65.7% (95% CI 59.4-71.5; 3 annotators, 256 images) and the average individual human 60.2%. GPT-5.4, the only proprietary model tested, scores 51.6% and ranks 11th of 18, below ten open-weight configurations including Qwen3.5 4B (56.1%). Size is a weak predictor: Kimi-VL (about 3B active parameters) at 52.4% ties InternVL3.5 38B at 52.6%, although within each dense family the largest model is the best, so family and training data matter more than size. Q-Bench+ (GPT-4V era): GPT-4V 74.10%, untrained humans 74.31%, experienced humans 81.74%. Corroboration from verifier notes only, not separately voted: GS-IQA severity accuracy is 0.677 for Qwen3-VL-235B, 0.563 for Gemini-3-Pro, 0.400 for GPT-5 and 0.363 for Gemini-2.5-Pro; Q-Bench-Portrait puts Qwen3-VL-32B (64.00) ahead of Grok-4 (62.51), Claude Sonnet 4.5 (60.42) and GPT-5.2 (56.67). Project note: the local pilot script /wanqing-develop/luowenjing/18/code/decision_eval/run_vllm_judge_pilot.py names its model qwen38-27b, so the 27B already tried appears to be in the family and size class that tops this benchmark (inferred from the script name only).

findings.claim: Severity grading, especially at adjacent and middle grades, is the weakest low-level skill of prompted VLMs. Their exact-grade error is about that of one human annotator, so a prompted VLM adds another noisy rater and does not resolve adjacent-grade ambiguity. They are most reliable at the severe end.
findings.evidence: DistortBench: the best model drops to 55.7% and 54.4% at severity levels 2-3 against 73.0% at level 5; GPT-5.4 scores 38.4% at level 1 and 72.9% at level 5 (parity with the best model at the severe end); human consensus also dips at level 2 (53.8%). Q-Doc: zero-shot 3-level severity grading of a named distortion peaks at 68.89% raw / 50.86% balanced accuracy (GPT-4o), and no model of six exceeds 70% on any split. Hallucination Score: rubric-prompted GPT-4o on a 1-5 scale matches the human majority grade on 29.0% of samples and is within one grade on 79.7%; its Spearman with the human mean is 0.56 against inter-human 0.54, and human-human exact agreement is 34.1%. Q-Bench+: graded 'How' questions are the lowest-scoring type for GPT-4V (66.45%) and for humans (60.29% untrained, 72.02% experienced). Wu et al. (ECCV 2024): GPT-4V is weak at discriminating fine-grained quality variations. None of these tests per-defect ordinal grading under a human labelling convention, so the transfer to this task is by proxy.

findings.claim: AI-restoration and over-generation artifacts are the hardest case for prompted models and for off-the-shelf quality scorers, and the only human-level prompted result needed the ground-truth image. The no-reference setting of this project is worse.
findings.evidence: Hallucination Score: GPT-4o reaches Spearman 0.56 with the human mean when given the low-resolution input, the super-resolved output and the ground truth; without the ground truth it falls to 0.47 (human mean) and 0.42 (majority). LL-Bench: zero-shot 7-8B open VLMs reach only 0.56-0.64 accuracy on binary hallucination detection across five restoration tasks, against 0.61-0.82 for the fine-tuned LL-Score; per-task test sets are tiny (about 28-49 images). Off-the-shelf scorers Q-Align, DeQA-Score and FGResQ reach overall SRCC 0.33-0.35 with human preference against 0.66 for LL-Score, though on the super-resolution task the gap is smaller (FGResQ 0.656 vs LL-Score 0.735). DistortBench: denoising artifacts are the hardest distortion, 26.2% mean accuracy across models against 25% chance, while humans scored 5 of 6 on them. No frontier closed-source model has been tested no-reference on over-generation, and no source covers cut-out background blur.

findings.claim: Where in-domain labels exist, fine-tuned specialists beat prompted frontier VLMs by wide margins, and fine-tuning a 7-8B open VLM beats prompting a closed model. A small encoder trained with pair supervision can match or beat fine-tuned VLM scorers.
findings.evidence: DepictQA-Wild (7B + LoRA): distortion-type accuracy 97.9% / 94.7% against GPT-4V 46.7% / 45.2% (82.1% / 73.2% on held-out distortion types); pairwise 'which is better' 90.3% / 89.8% against GPT-4V 77.8% / 75.2%, which is below PSNR (80.2%) and MUSIQ (76.9%). Co-Instruct (7B) reaches 77.12% single and 80.18% pair on Q-Bench+ against GPT-4V 74.10% and 78.07%, and against 62.68% and 48.94% for the same model untuned. Hallucination Score: Qwen2.5-VL-7B goes from Spearman 0.43 untuned to 0.70 fine-tuned, against 0.56 for GPT-4o. LL-Score is Qwen3-VL-8B with LoRA; the same model zero-shot scores 0.50-0.64 on hallucination detection. On NR-KADID, in-domain LIQE reaches SRCC 0.866 against GPT-4V 0.513. FGResQ (CLIP ViT-B/16 with a comparison head) reaches 0.752 fine-grained pair accuracy against 0.680 for DeQA-Score and 0.648 for Q-Align; excluding deraining the gap is about 1.6 points and on super-resolution it is a tie. Limits: these models trained on 30K-495K samples, not 3,500; most closed baselines are GPT-4V or GPT-4o; project memory records that FGResQ was already tried here without gain.

findings.claim: Teacher distillation from a VLM has evidence only where no human labels existed and the teacher was at human level. There is no evidence it helps when a few thousand human labels and a strong fine-tuned student already exist, and there is a documented case of the VLM being too weak to serve as a perceptual labeller.
findings.evidence: Hallucination Score: students trained only on 30,245 GPT-4o-labelled tuples correlate better with humans than the teacher (DINO-HS 0.71 / 0.63 and Qwen-HS 0.70 / 0.62 Spearman against human mean / majority, teacher 0.56 / 0.51). The setting is full-reference, the test set is 276 images, there is no baseline trained on human labels, and the untuned DINO feature distance already reaches 0.57. Co-Instruct's training set includes about 260K GPT-4V teacher responses and the student outperforms its teacher. Failure case: the DepictQA-Wild authors did not trust GPT-4V for low-level labels. They gave it ground-truth distortion labels and used it for wording, and trained their own assistant model for comparison labels, which beat GPT-4V on three unseen datasets (TID2013 94.9 / 94.6 vs 84.4 / 88.1; LIVE-MD 93.1 / 92.8 vs 79.6 / 72.7; MDID2013 90.1 / 89.8 vs 70.6 / 67.6). Inference for this project: the ensemble already detects at AUC about 0.95 and a prompted teacher's exact-grade noise equals human noise, so distilled grades would likely add noise unless the teacher first beats the ensemble's adjacent-grade AUC on held-out frames.

findings.claim: Pairwise comparison is the prompted mode with the most support: the strongest closed model and humans are both more accurate comparing two images than judging one. It still did not reach fine-tuned specialists, and it remained weak on fine-grained pairs.
findings.evidence: Q-Bench+: GPT-4V scores 78.07% on image pairs against 74.10% on single images, and 81.00% on the Compare subset against 80.26% for untrained and 86.55% for experienced humans; humans also improve on pairs (74.31% to 80.12%). Gemini-Pro and Qwen-VL-Max got worse on pairs, and untuned open models of that era were poor comparators (best 53.15% against 39.82% chance) until fine-tuned on comparison data (Co-Instruct 80.18%). Wu et al. (ECCV 2024): GPT-4V's best protocol is pairwise presentation with chain-of-thought (NR-KADID SRCC 0.639 vs 0.517 single; AGIQA-3K 0.771 vs 0.677), open models do best with single images, and showing several images at once degrades sharply. Against specialists, pairwise GPT-4V stays behind (77.8% / 75.2% vs 90.3% / 89.8%); on ranking restoration outputs it scores 74.5% against MUSIQ 77.3% and DepictQA-Wild 82.7% on about five test cases, with a spread of ±0.27 in rank across shuffled runs at temperature 0. A verifier note cites the 2AFC study where GPT-4V scored 0.244 against a human's 0.692 on fine-grained CSIQ pairs. All of this is GPT-4V era and not a controlled pairwise-versus-absolute test; no current frontier model has been tested on pairwise severity.

findings.claim: In-context grading with labelled exemplars and a written rubric has no surviving evidence for or against, and the practical questions on cost, latency and API image resolution are not answered by any verified claim.
findings.vote: In-context claim rejected 0-3; resolution and variance points come from claims 7 and 9 (3-0)
findings.evidence: The only claim about few-shot in-context exemplars (that they did not help GPT-4V) was rejected in verification, so this option is untested by the evidence base; the nearest result is rubric-prompted zero-shot GPT-4o in the severity finding above. On resolution, the Q-Bench+ authors attribute weak distortion perception partly to input down-sampling, but as a hypothesis with no ablation. On reasoning mode, DistortBench found thinking variants scored lower than base in 4 of 5 open-model pairs (Qwen3.5 27B 61.9% base vs 58.2% thinking), and GPT-5.4's reasoning setting was not reported. On stability, GPT-4V's answers varied across order-shuffled runs at temperature 0. Full pairwise protocols need a number of calls that grows with the square of the image count unless comparisons are made against a fixed set of anchors.

findings.claim: Conclusion: direct prompted grading and blind teacher distillation are the least supported uses; an offline anchored pairwise judge for adjacent-grade adjudication is the most defensible, and it should be gated by a pilot of under roughly ten thousand calls per model on held-out validation frames. This finding is a recommendation derived from the evidence above, not a published result.
findings.vote: Derived from the findings above; not separately voted
findings.evidence: Pilot design. Data: 300-400 human-labelled frames from validation folds only (never the 150-frame test set, per project rule 2), stratified toward adjacent-grade boundaries where the ensemble's out-of-fold prediction is uncertain and over-sampling over-generation; about 100 of them re-labelled by a second annotator to measure the human ceiling. Candidates: the local 27B as baseline plus two or three HTTP models chosen by measured low-level results, not size (the largest Qwen3-VL / Qwen3.5 variant, Gemini 3 Pro, one GPT-5.x, one Claude), each with reasoning off and on. Modes: (a) absolute rubric grade per defect; (b) rubric plus two or three labelled exemplars per grade; (c) anchored pairwise, where the test frame is compared with three or four anchor frames of known grade ('which shows more of defect X'), in both orders, aggregated to a score. Inputs: native-resolution tiles plus a full-frame view, each query repeated three times to measure consistency. Metrics: per-defect adjacent-grade AUC against the ensemble's out-of-fold score on the same frames (0.80 overall, 0.70 for over-generation); the gain from stacking the VLM score onto the ensemble logit under nested cross-validation with bootstrap intervals and three control seeds; agreement with the second annotator. Gates: use the model as judge or re-labeller only if it alone matches the ensemble's adjacent-grade AUC or the stacking gain exceeds seed noise and holds on a blind split; consider distillation only after that gate passes; otherwise stop. Size: 300 frames x 6 defects for modes (a) and (b), plus pairwise on the two weakest defects at about 8 calls each, is about 8,400 calls per model. A harness for this already exists at /wanqing-develop/luowenjing/18/code/decision_eval/run_http_judge_pilot.py; its header says results are comparable with the local 27B and the ensemble's out-of-fold predictions and that nothing is sent without an explicit flag. I read only its header, not its logic.

caveats:
Coverage of current models is thin. Most comparisons with specialists use GPT-4V or GPT-4o; only DistortBench covers a GPT-5-class model, and no voted claim tests Gemini 2.5/3, Claude, or any open model above 38B. The conclusion is therefore absence of evidence that a closed-source or larger model helps, not proof that it cannot.

Task mismatch is large. The benchmarks are multiple-choice questions on synthetic KADID-style distortions or correlations with overall quality scores. None grades six defects on an ordinal scale under a human labelling convention, none uses enhanced short-video frames, none covers cut-out background blur, and the over-generation evidence comes from super-resolution hallucination scored with a reference image.

Source quality varies. DistortBench is a workshop preprint; LL-Bench, Q-Doc and Hallucination Score are preprints in which authors evaluate their own methods. Several test sets are very small (276 images; about 28-49 per task in LL-Bench; about five cases for restoration ranking). The claim that closed-source status gives no advantage passed 2-1, not unanimously.

Some supporting numbers (GS-IQA, Q-Bench-Portrait, the 2AFC study, Co-Instruct details) come from verifier notes and were not voted on as separate claims; treat them as indicative.

The fine-tuning evidence used 30K-495K training samples, far more than the 3,500 labelled frames here, so the size of the gain may not transfer.

The question on API cost, latency and image-resolution limits is unanswered: no verified claim covers it. The in-context grading option is also unanswered, because its only claim was rejected.

The identification of the project's 27B pilot model as Qwen-family rests on a script name only.

Sending frames to an external HTTP endpoint is a data-handling decision for the owner, and any pilot must keep thresholds and model selection on validation and blind splits, not the 150-frame test set.

This field moves quickly; results for models released after mid-2026 could change the ranking.
openQuestions: Do Gemini 3-class, Claude or GPT-5.x models, given native-resolution crops and anchor frames, beat the ensemble's adjacent-grade AUC (0.80 overall, 0.70 for over-generation) on this project's held-out frames? No publication tests this.

Does anchored pairwise judging work for over-generation without a reference image, given that the only human-level prompted result (GPT-4o, Spearman 0.56) needed the ground truth and fell to 0.47 without it?
What resolution do the candidate HTTP endpoints actually pass to the model, and does tiling at native resolution recover the fine-texture evidence that down-scaling is suspected of destroying?

Is the adjacent-grade ceiling set by label noise and not by model capacity, so that double-annotating a subset would show the ensemble is already near human-human agreement and no judge model could add much?

refuted.claim: Few-shot in-context exemplars did not improve quality assessment: in-context prompting did not help GPT-4V under single-stimulus prompting, was unlikely to help the three open-source MLLMs, and caused a sharp performance drop in the multiple-stimulus setting with eight images. This weakens the case for an in-context grader with labelled exemplars (as of GPT-4V-era models).
